# adss

An **Analytical Data Storage System**, built as [blog.daana.dev](https://blog.daana.dev)
describes one: three layers, one direction of flow, and no shortcuts between them.

| Layer | Schemas | What it does | Engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DAS** — data according to the *system* | `das__raw`, `das__staged` | captures the source as it arrived, persists it append-only, unpacks it strictly per contract | [dlt](https://dlthub.com) → hive-partitioned parquet → DuckDB views |
| **DAB** — data according to the *business* | `dab`, `dab__stage`, `dab__meta` | the integrated business model, and the only place the data is explained | `daana-cli` focal model |
| **DAR** — data according to the *requirements* | `dar__uss` | a **generated** Unified Star Schema: one event bridge, one peripheral per entity, one calendar | the ADSS USS generator |

Destinations read `dar__uss` and nothing else.

The layer names are not decoration. They are the principles — see
[docs/blueprint.md](docs/blueprint.md).

## Status

Slice 0: the scaffold. The layers, the questions that accept them, and the skills that describe
them arrive in the slices that follow.

## Getting started

```bash
uv sync --all-groups
uv run adss --version
uv run pytest
uv run pre-commit run --all-files
```

## Slices

Each slice answers one business question, and the presentation of that answer is what the slice
is accepted on. It is the prototype, not a report generated afterwards.

| # | Question | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many orders were placed per order month and ship country? | not started |

| [docs/blueprint.md](docs/blueprint.md) | the principles, technology-free, no exceptions |
| [docs/conventions.md](docs/conventions.md) | the one convention document: naming, SQL, YAML, Python, commits |

--- 2 [ observed ] APPROACH B WINS: `@dlt.resource(columns={"payload": {"data_type": "json"}})` yielding a real dict under `payload` keeps the whole record in ONE column of dlt type `json`. No columns are inferred from inside it.

--- 4 [ observed ] APPROACH A also works: pre-serialising with json.dumps() gives a `text` column that DuckDB's JSON operators read identically. It is physically indistinguishable from B in parquet.
--- 5 [ observed ] APPROACH C FAILS the requirement: `max_table_nesting=0` does NOT stop normalisation. Top-level keys are still split into snake_cased typed columns; it only collapses NESTED values into json strings instead of child tables.
--- 6 [ observed ] 120 real Northwind Orders records (2 pages x $top=60 with $skip) landed to local filesystem parquet. The API reports @odata.count=830 total.
--- 7 [ observed ] Default filesystem layout is <bucket_url>/<dataset>/<table>/<load_id>.<file_id>.parquet — one parquet file per table per load, plus an `init` marker and three _dlt_* bookkeeping folders.
--- 8 [ observed ] DESCRIBE of the landed parquet from DuckDB: payload is VARCHAR, dlt `timestamp` becomes TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, `bigint` becomes BIGINT.
--- 9 [ observed ] dlt adds EXACTLY TWO metadata columns to a root table: `_dlt_load_id` and `_dlt_id`. Nothing else. They are NOT sufficient for 'which load, from where, when'.
--- 10 [ observed ] `_dlt_load_id` is only a unix-timestamp-ish string; the load's completion time and schema name live in a SEPARATE `_dlt_loads/*.jsonl` file — written as JSONL even when loader_file_format='parquet'. It is joinable but requires read_json_auto.
--- 11 [ observed ] `_dlt_id` is a per-row-instance surrogate, NOT a stable record identity. The same source record (OrderId 10248) got a different _dlt_id in each load. Content identity must come from your own hash column.
--- 12 [ observed ] write_disposition='append' leaves earlier files intact. Two runs of the identical pipeline produced two parquet files per table and two rows in _dlt_loads; nothing was overwritten.
--- 13 [ observed ] CRITICAL: dataset_name='das__raw' is silently normalised to 'das_raw' (double underscore collapsed). Passing enable_dataset_name_normalization=False on the destination preserves the literal 'das__raw' folder.
--- 14 [ observed ] CRITICAL: a plain read_parquet glob over an append-only lake SILENTLY DROPS columns added in later loads — no error, just missing data. `union_by_name => true` fixes it.
--- 15 [ observed ] DuckDB JSON operators work directly on the VARCHAR payload column with an implicit cast — no explicit ::JSON needed. `->>` yields VARCHAR (then CAST), `->` yields JSON, plus json_keys / json_array_length / json_extract.

--- 17 [ observed ] Hive-style date partitioning works via the filesystem `layout` parameter, but the placeholder names are {YYYY}/{MM}/{DD}, not {year}/{month}/{day}.
--- 18 [ observed ] Your own provenance columns pass through untouched, including names with leading underscores and a non-normalised prefix like `das_`. Timestamps land as dlt `timestamp` -> parquet -> DuckDB TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE.

Fix: dlt.destinations.filesystem(bucket_url=..., enable_dataset_name_normalization=False). If DAS/DAB/DAR all use double-underscore schema names, every dlt destination in the project needs this flag.

**Why the acquisition question has only one honest answer: the binary has no version.**

`daana-cli -v` prints `daana-cli version nightly, commit 113d5a6a77c123679656a9c769c6b88123341f36, built at 2026-09-04T22:13:46Z`. There is no semantic version to depend on. You cannot write "requires daana-cli >= 0.7.0" and have it mean anything, because the artefact does not claim to be 0.7.0. It claims to be *nightly*, which is a name for "whatever was on the branch that night". Every acquisition option therefore has to answer the same question — *which bytes* — and only two mechanisms can answer it: carry the bytes, or record their hash. The `.sha256` sitting beside the binary makes the second one free, and I verified it resolves against the copy present here (`492ddf86ab3361104f503a6e0cc9ce412ec6dfbcc744e7c30ae23eb0ccc739d3`, `sha256sum` agrees). That single fact — *no version exists, only content* — is what makes "content-pinned manifest" not one option among several but the shape any workable option has to take. The remaining choice is only *where the bytes live between commits*, and that is a much smaller question than it looks.

**Vendoring it via LFS, argued properly.** This is the option with the best failure mode and I want to be fair to it. `git clone` gives you a working system with no second step, no cache to warm, no network call at build time that can fail on a Tuesday. The pin is the repository itself; the review of an engine upgrade is a diff of an LFS pointer, which is exactly as reviewable as a hash in a manifest. There is no "it worked on my machine" because there is only one machine's worth of bytes. Against a 174 MB object the cost is not disk — disk is free — it is three other things. First, GitHub's LFS bandwidth is metered and `actions/checkout` with `lfs: true` pulls the object on **every** run; at 174 MB the free tier is exhausted in single-digit CI runs, and the failure is a billing failure in the middle of a slice, not a build failure you can debug. Second, an LFS object is permanent: every engine upgrade adds another 174 MB to the repository's storage forever, and this repository expects to outlive the tool by design ("Every tool this system currently uses must be replaceable without invalidating a single line below", blueprint.md). Carrying the tool inside the artefact that is supposed to survive its replacement is the wrong shape. Third, it makes this repository a redistribution point for someone else's unversioned nightly build, whose licence we have not established. None of those is fatal alone. Together they are enough, and the thing they buy — "no network at build time" — is a property we do not actually have anyway, because CI already reaches PyPI on every run via `uv sync --frozen`.

**Fetching unpinned, argued properly.** Simplest possible machinery: one `git clone --branch binaries`, done. It has one genuine virtue nobody else has — you cannot rot, because you always have the newest fix for whatever DuckDB bug bites next, and this engine has DuckDB bugs (see below). Against that: a branch called `binaries` carrying nightly builds is a branch that will be force-pushed. The day it is, the DAB layer changes underneath a green history, and `git bisect` — which conventions.md §7 makes load-bearing ("Bisect is only worth anything if every point in history is a working system") — starts lying, because the same commit now builds a different warehouse. Unpinned fetch is not a different option from pinned fetch; it is pinned fetch with the pin deleted.

**Local path only, argued properly.** Honest about where the binary actually comes from — someone put it there — and it costs zero machinery. It is also the only option that works in a genuinely airgapped environment. But it does not answer the question that was asked, which is "CI has to work". CI has never seen the binary; something has to put it on the runner, and "a documented manual step" on a hosted ephemeral runner is not a step, it is a wish. What it *is* good for is the escape hatch, so I keep it: `DAANA_CLI` pointing at a path, still hash-verified against the same manifest. The verification is what turns it from a story into a contract.

**Container image, argued properly.** The strongest reproducibility of the five: a digest-pinned image pins the binary *and* the glibc it was linked against, and a 174 MB Go binary from an unknown build environment is exactly the kind of thing that fails on the wrong base image. `docker run` in CI is one line. Two things sink it. It pins nothing extra unless you pin the digest, which is the same hash-in-a-manifest discipline one layer further out with more moving parts; and it makes Docker a prerequisite for a project whose entire toolchain is otherwise `uv sync`, for the sake of running one statically-linked executable. daana-cli 0.7.0 removed its own Docker sidecar ("Everything now runs inside the Go binary itself. The local Postgres sidecar is gone - no external database, no Docker port, no second process") — reintroducing a container to run the binary that was made containerless is moving against the tool's own grain. Revisit if the binary turns out to have runtime library dependencies we cannot satisfy on a plain runner.

**Writing the focal generator ourselves, argued properly, because it deserves it.** This is not a strawman. Look at what we are proposing to depend on: a binary that self-reports as `nightly`; whose `--help` advertises "Multi-database support (PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, Oracle, SQL Server)" and does *not* list DuckDB; whose 0.7.0 release post names PostgreSQL and BigQuery as the only tested environments; which creates `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` tables on DuckDB and never populates them while reporting the `execute_idfr_pipelines` phase as succeeding; which corrupts a base table by one row per run under a strategy the user selected, invisibly; and which reports "the framework is not installed" when the real problem is a file lock. Writing it ourselves would give us a generator we can test, a physical model we control, and no acquisition problem at all. What sinks it is the blueprint, not the effort: "Structure enforces the consistent application of business definitions; it does not produce the definitions... The effort saved on mechanism is meant to be redirected to meaning, not removed" (design-of-analytical-systems). Building the mechanism is precisely the effort the architecture wants redirected. And what we would be reimplementing is not trivial: spike 2 showed `view_CUSTOMER_hist` is a genuine gaps-and-islands window reconstruction that carries unchanged attributes forward across value-runs and aligns attributes sourced from *different tables under different ingestion strategies* onto the same `eff_tmstp`. That is the hard part of ensemble modelling and it works. We take the engine and we cage it.

**The cage is the real decision.** Every one of the engine's defects above is silent. None of them fails a build. That is what makes a numbered rule set the substance of this record rather than an appendix to it: daana accepts wrong mappings without complaint, so the honesty of the DAB layer is exactly equal to the rules we impose on the mapping files plus the tests that check them.

Rule M4 — `ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG` everywhere, `FULL` forbidden outright — is the one that had to be got right, and the two spikes settle it jointly rather than separately. Spike 1 established that `das__staged` is append-style *by construction*: "Two identical runs produce 240 rows for 120 distinct orders." Spike 2 established what `FULL` does to such a source: "customers mapping switched to `ingestion_strategy: FULL` while `das__staged.customers` held 2 rows for C001... run4: 23, run5: 24, run6: 25 (+1 every execute)... `view_CUSTOMER` stayed at 3 rows and `view_CUSTOMER_hist` at 4 rows throughout — the corruption never surfaces in the views." Unbounded growth, invisible to every consumer, and "switching back to FULL_LOG stops the growth but does NOT clean up the 5 rows already leaked." The obvious alternative — make `das__staged` a latest-per-key snapshot so that `FULL` becomes correct, which spike 2 finding 10 proves it is against a one-row-per-key view — must be rejected on principle, not on taste. It would make DAB's history a function of *how often the build ran* rather than of what DAS holds, and a cold rebuild would collapse every entity to a single version. Blueprint S2 exists for exactly this: "DAB and DAR must be rebuildable from DAS at any time without going back to the source." A snapshot staging view breaks S2 in the only way that matters. So the staged view keeps every version, and `FULL` is therefore unusable here, permanently, not situationally. `TRANSACTIONAL` (proven working in spike 2 finding 17) and `INCREMENTAL` are deferred rather than forbidden, because both introduce warehouse-resident watermark state and the abort path documented in `execute --help` ("If batch_history has prior 'F' or 'R' rows but no successful 'C' row... the framework aborts that pipeline"), which trades our reproducibility property for a speed we do not need at 830 orders.

The remaining rules follow from the same principle — that anything the engine will silently accept must be forbidden by us or asserted by a test. M6/M7 (expression purity) exist because a `transformation_expression` is inlined verbatim into generated SQL: a subquery there is a hand-written join, which contradicts "You don't write the joins - the model does" (why-we-built-daana), and an aggregate there is aggregation inside DAB, which contradicts B5. M3 (one `primary_keys` list per entity, identical across every table block) exists because spike 2 finding 14 showed `<entity>_key` is the natural key value verbatim — `'C001'`, `'O100'` — with `_idfr` empty, so there is no identifier-resolution layer to catch two table blocks that disagree about what identifies an instance; the mistake would just create two orders. M14 (the DAR allow-list) exists because three separate DuckDB-specific findings all point the same way: `_focal` and `_idfr` are created and never populated, so a DAR generator that joins to them returns nothing and reports zero rather than failing; `view_<entity>_with_rel` has a column list "byte-identical to `view_<entity>`", so its name is an active lie; and the presentation views wrap DuckDB table macros invisible to `information_schema`, so any name-construction or inventory code has to look in `duckdb_functions()` too. M16 turns that last one into a general rule: *names are looked up, never constructed*.

**On UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, which is the question I expected to answer the other way.** The case against keeping it is real and I will state it at full strength. daana-cli 0.7.0 explicitly relaxed the requirement — "Entity IDs, workflow IDs, attribute names, and relationship names now accept any casing... The checker and compiler previously enforced UPPER_SNAKE_CASE" — and removed the three lint rules that enforced it, so the tool no longer supports the convention at all. Spike 2 then showed the consequence on our platform: DuckDB preserves the casing, giving `view_CUSTOMER`, `CUSTOMER_desc`, `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x`, where PostgreSQL folds the same model to lowercase. So the same `model.yaml` produces differently-named objects on two platforms — in a system whose stated design is "platform behind one seam". Lowercasing the model ids would erase that difference, erase the two-casing world, let `RF06` back into sqlfluff (it is currently excluded, and it is a correctness rule, not a style rule), and mean no identifier anywhere ever needs a quote. That is a genuinely strong case and it nearly wins.

It loses on two counts. The first is that the portability benefit is already bought elsewhere: rule M16 requires every DAB object name to be *read from the catalog and compared case-insensitively*, a rule I need anyway because of the table macros and the empty `_focal` tables. Once no name is constructed, the platform difference is unobservable, and spike 2 confirmed the consumer side is safe regardless — `dab.view_customer`, `dab.VIEW_CUSTOMER`, `dab."view_CUSTOMER"` and `dab."view_customer"` all resolve to the same object. The second is the argument conventions.md itself makes: the visual break is what makes a leak obvious on sight. There is exactly one file in this system where business vocabulary and source vocabulary appear on the same line — the mapping. `{id: SHIP_COUNTRY, transformation_expression: ship_country}` is legible at a glance in a way `{id: ship_country, transformation_expression: ship_country}` is not, and mapping edits are the highest-frequency change in the DAB layer. §1.2's hard rule against source names in DAB has no mechanical enforcement now that daana's lint rules are gone; the casing break is the cheapest thing that makes a violation visible to a reviewer. Decisive corroboration that the convention was written knowing this: `.sqlfluff` already excludes RF06 with the comment "RF06 fires on every mixed-case identifier crossing over from DAB", and §3 already says "Identifiers crossing over from DAB are double-quoted". The cost of mixed-case DAB identifiers was priced into this repository before the spike ran. The convention survives contact. It is not free, and I record the price in the consequences.

**Single-writer discipline.** Spike 2 finding 11 is the most operationally dangerous thing either spike found, because it is a correct-looking wrong answer: with any other connection open — "read-write OR READ-ONLY" — `execute` fails with "daana framework is not installed on the remote database. Run 'daana-cli install' first", and "no 'lock', 'conflict' or 'duckdb' string appears anywhere in the debug output". An operator who believes that message runs `install`, which will fail the same way, and the obvious next move is to start deleting schemas. The design response is two-part and both parts are machinery, so both are test-first. First, prevention: one build process holds an exclusive `flock` on `warehouse.duckdb.lock` for its whole run, and the platform seam grows an explicit *detached* state — every Python DuckDB connection is closed and asserted closed before the engine subprocess is spawned, and reopened afterwards. daana-cli is the only writer during its own phase because it is structurally the only holder. Second, translation: the subprocess wrapper matches the known stderr string and replaces it with a message naming the file, the real cause, the fact that other *readers* count, and the explicit instruction that `install` is not the fix. That translation is generic machinery with no data vocabulary in it (conventions §5), which means it can be unit-tested against the recorded stderr — and must be, because the string comes from a nightly binary and will eventually be reworded, at which point the test fails and tells us, rather than the translation silently going quiet.

consequences.text: DAB becomes a pure function of das__staged plus the YAML. No watermark, no run history, no ambient config participates in what the warehouse contains, so "build it twice, get the same thing" is an assertion rather than an aspiration — and it is the assertion that catches the FULL-class corruption, which no view will ever show.

The engine has an identity for the first time. `nightly` is not a version, but sha256 plus the self-reported commit is, and both are checked on every invocation, so "it worked on my machine" is falsifiable in one command and an engine change is a one-line reviewable diff in `dab/engine.lock`.

The three DuckDB-specific traps — empty `_focal`/`_idfr`, table macros invisible to information_schema, and `_with_rel` carrying no relationship keys — are converted from folklore into a named allow-list and a lookup-don't-construct rule, so a future DAR generator cannot rediscover them by returning a plausible zero.

The misleading "framework is not installed" error is translated once, in machinery, under test. No operator will ever run `daana-cli install` against a busy file and start deleting schemas to make it work.

Keeping UPPER_SNAKE_CASE keeps the one file where business and source vocabulary meet — the mapping — legible at a glance, which is the only remaining enforcement of "no source name appears anywhere in DAB" now that daana-cli 0.7.0 has deleted its casing lint rules.

FULL_LOG re-reads the entire retained history of das__staged on every execute. At 830 Northwind orders this is free; at the first source with a daily full extract, execute time grows linearly with days retained and never comes back down. The escape — TRANSACTIONAL or INCREMENTAL — costs us the reproducibility property above and buys the batch_history abort path documented in `execute --help` (prior 'F'/'R' rows with no 'C' abort the pipeline and need manual repair), so the fix for the slow build is strictly worse than the build.

We have engineered FULL_LOG's soft-delete into never firing. It deletes when a key disappears from the source view; our staged view is append-only over the whole lake, so a key never disappears. An order deleted at the source stays in `dab.view_ORDER` forever and nothing in the build will say so. We have chosen a mechanism whose delete semantics are structurally unreachable, and no test can detect the miss, because the correct answer is indistinguishable from the wrong one without going back to the source — which S2 forbids.

The build is now strictly serial and hostile to a human being present. A marimo page left open, an editor's database viewer, or a second developer's `duckdb` REPL turns a ten-second build into a failure, and the failure is only intelligible because of a string match against a nightly binary's error text that we now own and must keep in step. The day the vendor rewords that message, our test goes red and someone has to go and find out what the new wording is.

The engine is an unversioned nightly pinned by content hash on a branch we do not control. If that branch is force-pushed or the LFS object is garbage-collected, the pinned bytes become unfetchable and there is no upstream to ask for them — we have no version number with which to request the same build again. The mitigation (a cached copy, `DAANA_CLI` pointing at it) is a copy someone has to have kept.

The pin is `linux-amd64`. The DAB layer is verified on exactly one platform; a developer on macOS arm64 cannot build DAB at all until a second object is pinned, and the build must fail loudly rather than silently skipping the layer. This is a real barrier to a second person joining the work.

Keeping UPPER_SNAKE_CASE keeps two casing worlds, which is why `RF06` — table-qualification of column references, the one sqlfluff correctness rule that cannot be autofixed — stays excluded for *all* SQL in the repository, hand-written included. We pay that price on every file to buy legibility in the mapping files.

Banning `view_<ENTITY>_with_rel` means DAR gets relationship keys one relationship view at a time: n reads for n edges rather than one wide read per entity. Slice 1 has no relationships so the cost is zero now and grows with every edge added, and the ban is a rule rather than a mechanism — nothing in DuckDB stops someone reading `_focal` and getting a confident, empty, plausible answer.

`PLACED_ON` is declared `START_TIMESTAMP` because the DMDL vocabulary has no plain timestamp. If the engine treats START/END_TIMESTAMP as a validity interval rather than an instant, a `START_TIMESTAMP` with no matching `END_TIMESTAMP` may be rejected or may acquire behaviour we did not ask for. We are relying on a semantic reading of five type names, and the first slice is where we find out.

DAB is the layer the whole architecture exists for. It is where meaning is defined exactly once (blueprint B8), where change must be additive (B7), and where history must be retained such that an answer served last quarter is reproducible this quarter (B3). We have decided that daana-cli produces it, that `dab/model.yaml` is the only place the data is explained, and that the physical target is one DuckDB file. That decision is not in question here. What is in question is everything that makes it survivable: where the binary comes from, what a mapping file is allowed to say, who is allowed to have the file open, and what DAR is allowed to see of what the engine produced.

The first hard thing is that this engine has no version. Its own `-v` prints `daana-cli version nightly, commit 113d5a6a77c123679656a9c769c6b88123341f36, built at 2026-09-04T22:13:46Z`. There is no semver to depend on, no release to request again, and the artefact lives as a 174 MB git-LFS object on a branch called `binaries` in a repository we do not control. Its `--help` advertises "Multi-database support (PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, Oracle, SQL Server)" and does not list DuckDB. The 0.7.0 release post names PostgreSQL and BigQuery as the only tested environments. So the platform we have chosen is unadvertised, unsupported territory in an unversioned nightly build — and it works, fully, as spike 2 proved end to end. Everything below follows from taking that pair of facts seriously at the same time.

The second hard thing is that the engine accepts wrong mappings without complaining, and one class of wrongness corrupts the warehouse invisibly and irreversibly. Spike 2 set `ingestion_strategy: FULL` against a staged view holding two rows for one key and watched `CUSTOMER_desc` grow 22 → 23 → 24 → 25, one duplicate row per execute, forever — while `view_CUSTOMER` stayed at 3 rows and `view_CUSTOMER_hist` at 4 throughout. The corruption never reaches a consumer, so nothing downstream can detect it, and switching the strategy back stops the growth but does not clean up what leaked. This is not an exotic edge case in our design: spike 1 established that dlt's append disposition over a partitioned lake means `das__staged` holds more than one row per key *by construction* ("Two identical runs produce 240 rows for 120 distinct orders"). The default-looking strategy is the one that destroys the layer. That single fact determines the shape of this record: the honesty of DAB is exactly equal to the rules we impose on the mapping files, plus the tests that check them, because the engine will not.

The third hard thing is concurrency, and it is worse than it sounds. Spike 2 found that if any other process holds the `.duckdb` file open — "read-write OR READ-ONLY" — `daana-cli execute` fails with "daana framework is not installed on the remote database. Run 'daana-cli install' first", and the real lock error "is swallowed and does not appear even at `--log-level debug`". In this architecture the things that will hold that file open are the marimo page reading `dar__uss`, a dlt run, and a developer's REPL — i.e. the normal state of the world. An operator who believes the message will run `install` against a live warehouse. The problem is not just to serialise the build; it is that the diagnostic actively points at a destructive wrong answer.

The fourth is that the engine's physical output on DuckDB is partly a trap. `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` are created and never populated — zero rows for both entities — while `execute` still reports its `execute_idfr_pipelines` phase as succeeding. The presentation views are thin wrappers over DuckDB **table macros**, which do not appear in `information_schema.tables` at all. And `view_<entity>_with_rel`, whose name promises the relationship keys joined on, has a column list "byte-identical to `view_<entity>`" and carries none. Every one of those produces a plausible, silent, wrong answer rather than an error. DAR is generated code reading DAB; if it is written against the wrong objects it will emit zeroes with total confidence.

The fifth is a convention under pressure. conventions.md §1.2 makes UPPER_SNAKE_CASE with `id` == `name` a hard rule. daana-cli 0.7.0 removed its enforcement of exactly that — "Entity IDs, workflow IDs, attribute names, and relationship names now accept any casing" — and deleted the three lint rules that checked it. Spike 2 then showed what our platform does with it: DuckDB *preserves* the casing, producing `view_CUSTOMER`, `CUSTOMER_desc`, `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x`, where the same model on PostgreSQL folds to lowercase. So a rule the tool no longer supports now also produces platform-dependent object names in a system whose whole point is that the platform sits behind one seam. Either the convention earns its keep against that, or it should be superseded rather than left as folklore.

Whether the daana-cli licence permits redistribution. It bears directly on the rejected vendoring option and was not established; if redistribution is permitted and LFS bandwidth is later solved, vendoring becomes cheaper than it looks here.

data.argument:
**Why the acquisition question has only one honest answer: the binary has no version.**

`daana-cli -v` prints `daana-cli version nightly, commit 113d5a6a77c123679656a9c769c6b88123341f36, built at 2026-09-04T22:13:46Z`. There is no semantic version to depend on. You cannot write "requires daana-cli >= 0.7.0" and have it mean anything, because the artefact does not claim to be 0.7.0. It claims to be *nightly*, which is a name for "whatever was on the branch that night". Every acquisition option therefore has to answer the same question — *which bytes* — and only two mechanisms can answer it: carry the bytes, or record their hash. The `.sha256` sitting beside the binary makes the second one free, and I verified it resolves against the copy present here (`492ddf86ab3361104f503a6e0cc9ce412ec6dfbcc744e7c30ae23eb0ccc739d3`, `sha256sum` agrees). That single fact — *no version exists, only content* — is what makes "content-pinned manifest" not one option among several but the shape any workable option has to take. The remaining choice is only *where the bytes live between commits*, and that is a much smaller question than it looks.

**Vendoring it via LFS, argued properly.** This is the option with the best failure mode and I want to be fair to it. `git clone` gives you a working system with no second step, no cache to warm, no network call at build time that can fail on a Tuesday. The pin is the repository itself; the review of an engine upgrade is a diff of an LFS pointer, which is exactly as reviewable as a hash in a manifest. There is no "it worked on my machine" because there is only one machine's worth of bytes. Against a 174 MB object the cost is not disk — disk is free — it is three other things. First, GitHub's LFS bandwidth is metered and `actions/checkout` with `lfs: true` pulls the object on **every** run; at 174 MB the free tier is exhausted in single-digit CI runs, and the failure is a billing failure in the middle of a slice, not a build failure you can debug. Second, an LFS object is permanent: every engine upgrade adds another 174 MB to the repository's storage forever, and this repository expects to outlive the tool by design ("Every tool this system currently uses must be replaceable without invalidating a single line below", blueprint.md). Carrying the tool inside the artefact that is supposed to survive its replacement is the wrong shape. Third, it makes this repository a redistribution point for someone else's unversioned nightly build, whose licence we have not established. None of those is fatal alone. Together they are enough, and the thing they buy — "no network at build time" — is a property we do not actually have anyway, because CI already reaches PyPI on every run via `uv sync --frozen`.

**Fetching unpinned, argued properly.** Simplest possible machinery: one `git clone --branch binaries`, done. It has one genuine virtue nobody else has — you cannot rot, because you always have the newest fix for whatever DuckDB bug bites next, and this engine has DuckDB bugs (see below). Against that: a branch called `binaries` carrying nightly builds is a branch that will be force-pushed. The day it is, the DAB layer changes underneath a green history, and `git bisect` — which conventions.md §7 makes load-bearing ("Bisect is only worth anything if every point in history is a working system") — starts lying, because the same commit now builds a different warehouse. Unpinned fetch is not a different option from pinned fetch; it is pinned fetch with the pin deleted.

**Local path only, argued properly.** Honest about where the binary actually comes from — someone put it there — and it costs zero machinery. It is also the only option that works in a genuinely airgapped environment. But it does not answer the question that was asked, which is "CI has to work". CI has never seen the binary; something has to put it on the runner, and "a documented manual step" on a hosted ephemeral runner is not a step, it is a wish. What it *is* good for is the escape hatch, so I keep it: `DAANA_CLI` pointing at a path, still hash-verified against the same manifest. The verification is what turns it from a story into a contract.

**Container image, argued properly.** The strongest reproducibility of the five: a digest-pinned image pins the binary *and* the glibc it was linked against, and a 174 MB Go binary from an unknown build environment is exactly the kind of thing that fails on the wrong base image. `docker run` in CI is one line. Two things sink it. It pins nothing extra unless you pin the digest, which is the same hash-in-a-manifest discipline one layer further out with more moving parts; and it makes Docker a prerequisite for a project whose entire toolchain is otherwise `uv sync`, for the sake of running one statically-linked executable. daana-cli 0.7.0 removed its own Docker sidecar ("Everything now runs inside the Go binary itself. The local Postgres sidecar is gone - no external database, no Docker port, no second process") — reintroducing a container to run the binary that was made containerless is moving against the tool's own grain. Revisit if the binary turns out to have runtime library dependencies we cannot satisfy on a plain runner.

**Writing the focal generator ourselves, argued properly, because it deserves it.** This is not a strawman. Look at what we are proposing to depend on: a binary that self-reports as `nightly`; whose `--help` advertises "Multi-database support (PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, Oracle, SQL Server)" and does *not* list DuckDB; whose 0.7.0 release post names PostgreSQL and BigQuery as the only tested environments; which creates `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` tables on DuckDB and never populates them while reporting the `execute_idfr_pipelines` phase as succeeding; which corrupts a base table by one row per run under a strategy the user selected, invisibly; and which reports "the framework is not installed" when the real problem is a file lock. Writing it ourselves would give us a generator we can test, a physical model we control, and no acquisition problem at all. What sinks it is the blueprint, not the effort: "Structure enforces the consistent application of business definitions; it does not produce the definitions... The effort saved on mechanism is meant to be redirected to meaning, not removed" (design-of-analytical-systems). Building the mechanism is precisely the effort the architecture wants redirected. And what we would be reimplementing is not trivial: spike 2 showed `view_CUSTOMER_hist` is a genuine gaps-and-islands window reconstruction that carries unchanged attributes forward across value-runs and aligns attributes sourced from *different tables under different ingestion strategies* onto the same `eff_tmstp`. That is the hard part of ensemble modelling and it works. We take the engine and we cage it.

**The cage is the real decision.** Every one of the engine's defects above is silent. None of them fails a build. That is what makes a numbered rule set the substance of this record rather than an appendix to it: daana accepts wrong mappings without complaint, so the honesty of the DAB layer is exactly equal to the rules we impose on the mapping files plus the tests that check them.

Rule M4 — `ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG` everywhere, `FULL` forbidden outright — is the one that had to be got right, and the two spikes settle it jointly rather than separately. Spike 1 established that `das__staged` is append-style *by construction*: "Two identical runs produce 240 rows for 120 distinct orders." Spike 2 established what `FULL` does to such a source: "customers mapping switched to `ingestion_strategy: FULL` while `das__staged.customers` held 2 rows for C001... run4: 23, run5: 24, run6: 25 (+1 every execute)... `view_CUSTOMER` stayed at 3 rows and `view_CUSTOMER_hist` at 4 rows throughout — the corruption never surfaces in the views." Unbounded growth, invisible to every consumer, and "switching back to FULL_LOG stops the growth but does NOT clean up the 5 rows already leaked." The obvious alternative — make `das__staged` a latest-per-key snapshot so that `FULL` becomes correct, which spike 2 finding 10 proves it is against a one-row-per-key view — must be rejected on principle, not on taste. It would make DAB's history a function of *how often the build ran* rather than of what DAS holds, and a cold rebuild would collapse every entity to a single version. Blueprint S2 exists for exactly this: "DAB and DAR must be rebuildable from DAS at any time without going back to the source." A snapshot staging view breaks S2 in the only way that matters. So the staged view keeps every version, and `FULL` is therefore unusable here, permanently, not situationally. `TRANSACTIONAL` (proven working in spike 2 finding 17) and `INCREMENTAL` are deferred rather than forbidden, because both introduce warehouse-resident watermark state and the abort path documented in `execute --help` ("If batch_history has prior 'F' or 'R' rows but no successful 'C' row... the framework aborts that pipeline"), which trades our reproducibility property for a speed we do not need at 830 orders.

The remaining rules follow from the same principle — that anything the engine will silently accept must be forbidden by us or asserted by a test. M6/M7 (expression purity) exist because a `transformation_expression` is inlined verbatim into generated SQL: a subquery there is a hand-written join, which contradicts "You don't write the joins - the model does" (why-we-built-daana), and an aggregate there is aggregation inside DAB, which contradicts B5. M3 (one `primary_keys` list per entity, identical across every table block) exists because spike 2 finding 14 showed `<entity>_key` is the natural key value verbatim — `'C001'`, `'O100'` — with `_idfr` empty, so there is no identifier-resolution layer to catch two table blocks that disagree about what identifies an instance; the mistake would just create two orders. M14 (the DAR allow-list) exists because three separate DuckDB-specific findings all point the same way: `_focal` and `_idfr` are created and never populated, so a DAR generator that joins to them returns nothing and reports zero rather than failing; `view_<entity>_with_rel` has a column list "byte-identical to `view_<entity>`", so its name is an active lie; and the presentation views wrap DuckDB table macros invisible to `information_schema`, so any name-construction or inventory code has to look in `duckdb_functions()` too. M16 turns that last one into a general rule: *names are looked up, never constructed*.

**On UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, which is the question I expected to answer the other way.** The case against keeping it is real and I will state it at full strength. daana-cli 0.7.0 explicitly relaxed the requirement — "Entity IDs, workflow IDs, attribute names, and relationship names now accept any casing... The checker and compiler previously enforced UPPER_SNAKE_CASE" — and removed the three lint rules that enforced it, so the tool no longer supports the convention at all. Spike 2 then showed the consequence on our platform: DuckDB preserves the casing, giving `view_CUSTOMER`, `CUSTOMER_desc`, `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x`, where PostgreSQL folds the same model to lowercase. So the same `model.yaml` produces differently-named objects on two platforms — in a system whose stated design is "platform behind one seam". Lowercasing the model ids would erase that difference, erase the two-casing world, let `RF06` back into sqlfluff (it is currently excluded, and it is a correctness rule, not a style rule), and mean no identifier anywhere ever needs a quote. That is a genuinely strong case and it nearly wins.

It loses on two counts. The first is that the portability benefit is already bought elsewhere: rule M16 requires every DAB object name to be *read from the catalog and compared case-insensitively*, a rule I need anyway because of the table macros and the empty `_focal` tables. Once no name is constructed, the platform difference is unobservable, and spike 2 confirmed the consumer side is safe regardless — `dab.view_customer`, `dab.VIEW_CUSTOMER`, `dab."view_CUSTOMER"` and `dab."view_customer"` all resolve to the same object. The second is the argument conventions.md itself makes: the visual break is what makes a leak obvious on sight. There is exactly one file in this system where business vocabulary and source vocabulary appear on the same line — the mapping. `{id: SHIP_COUNTRY, transformation_expression: ship_country}` is legible at a glance in a way `{id: ship_country, transformation_expression: ship_country}` is not, and mapping edits are the highest-frequency change in the DAB layer. §1.2's hard rule against source names in DAB has no mechanical enforcement now that daana's lint rules are gone; the casing break is the cheapest thing that makes a violation visible to a reviewer. Decisive corroboration that the convention was written knowing this: `.sqlfluff` already excludes RF06 with the comment "RF06 fires on every mixed-case identifier crossing over from DAB", and §3 already says "Identifiers crossing over from DAB are double-quoted". The cost of mixed-case DAB identifiers was priced into this repository before the spike ran. The convention survives contact. It is not free, and I record the price in the consequences.

**Single-writer discipline.** Spike 2 finding 11 is the most operationally dangerous thing either spike found, because it is a correct-looking wrong answer: with any other connection open — "read-write OR READ-ONLY" — `execute` fails with "daana framework is not installed on the remote database. Run 'daana-cli install' first", and "no 'lock', 'conflict' or 'duckdb' string appears anywhere in the debug output". An operator who believes that message runs `install`, which will fail the same way, and the obvious next move is to start deleting schemas. The design response is two-part and both parts are machinery, so both are test-first. First, prevention: one build process holds an exclusive `flock` on `warehouse.duckdb.lock` for its whole run, and the platform seam grows an explicit *detached* state — every Python DuckDB connection is closed and asserted closed before the engine subprocess is spawned, and reopened afterwards. daana-cli is the only writer during its own phase because it is structurally the only holder. Second, translation: the subprocess wrapper matches the known stderr string and replaces it with a message naming the file, the real cause, the fact that other *readers* count, and the explicit instruction that `install` is not the fix. That translation is generic machinery with no data vocabulary in it (conventions §5), which means it can be unit-tested against the recorded stderr — and must be, because the string comes from a nightly binary and will eventually be reworded, at which point the test fails and tells us, rather than the translation silently going quiet.

**`dab/model.yaml`** — slice 1 has one entity and no `relationships:` block, because there is nothing yet for ORDER to relate to.

```yaml
entities:
  - id: "ORDER"
    name: "ORDER"
    definition: "A request from a customer for goods, accepted by the business as a commitment to supply them."
    description: "One order is one such commitment. It exists from the moment it is accepted."
    attributes:
      - id: "ORDER_ID"
        name: "ORDER_ID"
        definition: "The identifier the business uses when it refers to one order."
        type: "STRING"
        effective_timestamp: false
      - id: "PLACED_ON"
        name: "PLACED_ON"
        definition: "The moment the business accepted the order and it began to exist."
        type: "START_TIMESTAMP"
      - id: "SHIP_COUNTRY"
        name: "SHIP_COUNTRY"
        definition: "The country the business has undertaken to deliver the order to."
        type: "STRING"
        effective_timestamp: true
```

`type` values are constrained to `STRING`, `NUMBER`, `UNIT`, `START_TIMESTAMP`, `END_TIMESTAMP`. There is no plain timestamp type, so `PLACED_ON` takes `START_TIMESTAMP` — the entity's own beginning-of-life business instant, which is semantically what an order date is — and omits `effective_timestamp`, matching every START/END-typed attribute in the DMDL example. `ORDER_ID` carries `effective_timestamp: false` because it is the key.

---

**`dab/mappings/order-mapping.yaml`**

```yaml
entity_id: ORDER
mapping_groups:
  - name: default_mapping_group
    tables:
      - connection: dev
        table: das__staged.orders
        primary_keys: [order_id]
        ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG
        entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at
        attributes:
          - {id: ORDER_ID, transformation_expression: cast(order_id AS VARCHAR)}
          - {id: PLACED_ON, transformation_expression: order_date}
          - {id: SHIP_COUNTRY, transformation_expression: ship_country}
```

Flow mappings for the attribute rows are explicitly blessed by conventions §4 ("a mapping attribute") and unpadded, so a longer expression is a one-line diff. `.yamllint.yaml` sets `braces.max-spaces-inside: 1` and `line-length.max: 160`, so this passes the gate as written. The single `cast(...)` is the only kind permitted by M7 — the one needed to reach the declared DMDL type, spelled `cast(x AS T)` per conventions §3, never `::`.

---

```yaml
connections:

    type: duckdb
    database: ../warehouse.duckdb
    target_schema: dab
    stage_schema: dab__stage
    metadata_schema: dab__meta
```

`../warehouse.duckdb` resolves to the same file whether the engine resolves it against the process cwd or against `connections.yaml` — because M12 fixes cwd to `dab/`, which is where `connections.yaml` lives. ```yaml
workflow:
  id: "ADSS"
  name: "ADSS"
  model: "./model.yaml"
  connection: "dev"
  mappings:
    - "./mappings/order-mapping.yaml"
```

**`dab/engine.lock`** — the pin. Content-addressed, because there is no version.

```yaml
engine: daana-cli
source:
  repo: "https://github.com/mattiasthalen/ADSS-fable-POC"
  ref: "binaries"
  path: "bin/linux-amd64/daana-cli"
platform: "linux-amd64"
sha256: "492ddf86ab3361104f503a6e0cc9ce412ec6dfbcc744e7c30ae23eb0ccc739d3"
self_report: "daana-cli version nightly, commit 113d5a6a77c123679656a9c769c6b88123341f36, built at 2026-09-04T22:13:46Z"
```

Whichever path wins, both checks run before any invocation: `sha256` of the file equals `engine.lock`, and the binary's own `-v` output equals `self_report` verbatim. CI adds `actions/cache` keyed on the sha256, so the 174 MB fetch happens once per pin, not once per run.

daana-cli check mapping   --config ./config.yaml --no-tui --format json --skip-schema-validation   # gate: offline, no DB
daana-cli check mapping   --config ./config.yaml --no-tui --format json --connections ./connections.yaml --connection dev --strict

So the slice-1 DAR read, with DAB identifiers double-quoted per conventions §3:

```sql

    o."ORDER_key" AS order_key,
    o.order_id AS order_id,
    o.placed_on AS placed_on,
    o.ship_country AS ship_country
FROM dab.view_order AS o
```

```sql

WHERE table_schema IN ('dab', 'dab__stage', 'dab__meta');

SELECT schema_name, function_name, function_type FROM duckdb_functions()
WHERE schema_name IN ('dab', 'dab__stage', 'dab__meta');
```

|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | A mapping table's `table:` is exactly `das__staged.<contract stem>`. Never `das__raw`, never a path or `read_parquet()`, never a `dab` object. | Blueprint F3. `das__raw` is an untyped payload column; unpacking it from a mapping would move S3's strict boundary into the wrong layer. | Hard |

| M3 | The instance key is declared once, as `primary_keys:` naming the das__staged column(s) carrying the source's own key, identical in every table block of that entity. | M4 | `ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG` on every table. `FULL` is forbidden. `INCREMENTAL`/`TRANSACTIONAL` require an ADR. | `das__staged` is append-style by construction; `FULL` against it leaks one `_desc` row per execute, unbounded, invisible in every view. | Hard |
| M5 | `entity_effective_timestamp_expression:` is the bare column `extracted_at`. No expression, no `COALESCE`, no source business date. | Already decided; a business date makes `eff_tmstp` non-monotonic and makes "what did we know when" unanswerable. | Hard |
| M6 | A `transformation_expression` is a pure, single-row function of columns of its own table: no subquery, join, aggregate, window, cross-schema reference, or non-deterministic function. | It is inlined into generated SQL unchecked. A subquery is a hand-written join; an aggregate is aggregation inside DAB (B5). | Hard |
| M7 | It may name one column, optionally wrapped in the single `cast(x AS T)` needed to reach the declared DMDL type. | M8 | Do not cast numerics for width or scale. | Everything is materialised `DECIMAL(28,8)` regardless; the cast misleads the reader. Formatting is DAR's job. | Guideline |

The headline check is `tests/test_dab_build.py::test_cold_rebuild_is_complete_and_deterministic`, and it is a data check in the conventions §6 sense — it asserts what the built warehouse contains and lands with the build that satisfies it. It seeds `das/fixtures` with the same Northwind Orders recorded under **two** `extracted_on` partitions, the second changing `ShipCountry` on exactly one order, then builds the whole spine twice from empty, in one process, and asserts four things:

1. `SELECT count(*) FROM dab."ORDER_desc"` is identical after build 1 and build 2. This is the M4 canary: under `FULL` this number increments by one per execute while every view stays constant, so it is the only place the leak is observable.
2. `SELECT count(*) FROM dab.view_order_hist WHERE order_id = <the changed order>` is 2, with the two `eff_tmstp` values equal to the two `extracted_at` values derived from the fixture's `_dlt_load_id`s. This proves M5's dating *and* proves that `FULL_LOG` reconstructs history in a single cold execute rather than only accumulating it across runs — the one thing spike 2 did not isolate.
3. `SELECT count(*) FROM dab.view_order` equals the distinct order count, i.e. one row per order, not one per load.
4. The slice-1 answer computed from `dar__uss` equals the answer computed from `das__staged` — the two-computations rule, which here doubles as the end-to-end proof that the allow-listed views carry what DAR needs.

Three supporting checks, each cheap and each guarding a specific finding:

- `tests/test_engine_pin.py` — resolve the engine, assert its sha256 equals `dab/engine.lock`'s and that `daana-cli -v` output equals the recorded `self_report` string exactly. Fails the day the pin and the bytes diverge, whichever moved.
- `tests/test_mapping_rules.py` — parse every file in `dab/mappings/`, assert for every table block that `table` starts `das__staged.`, `ingestion_strategy` is `FULL_LOG`, `entity_effective_timestamp_expression` is `extracted_at`, `primary_keys` is identical across all blocks of one entity, and no `transformation_expression` matches `SELECT|JOIN|OVER\s*\(|\b(sum|count|avg|min|max|now|random)\s*\(`. Machinery only, no entity names in the test (conventions §5). This is M1/M3/M4/M5/M6 made mechanical.
- `tests/test_single_writer.py` — open a second **read-only** DuckDB connection to the warehouse, run the DAB phase, assert it fails with *our* busy-file message and that the message does not contain the word "install" as an instruction; and a second case feeding the recorded stderr string to the translator directly, so the translation is tested independently of the lock. The day a nightly binary rewords that error, this test goes red and tells us, instead of the translation silently going quiet.

Plus one review-time check that no test can perform: an ADR is required to introduce a second relationship between the same ordered entity pair (M11), because the collision would show up as missing rows, not as an error.

consequences.text: DAB becomes a pure function of das__staged plus the YAML. No watermark, no run history, no ambient config participates in what the warehouse contains, so "build it twice, get the same thing" is an assertion rather than an aspiration — and it is the assertion that catches the FULL-class corruption, which no view will ever show.

The engine has an identity for the first time. `nightly` is not a version, but sha256 plus the self-reported commit is, and both are checked on every invocation, so "it worked on my machine" is falsifiable in one command and an engine change is a one-line reviewable diff in `dab/engine.lock`.

The three DuckDB-specific traps — empty `_focal`/`_idfr`, table macros invisible to information_schema, and `_with_rel` carrying no relationship keys — are converted from folklore into a named allow-list and a lookup-don't-construct rule, so a future DAR generator cannot rediscover them by returning a plausible zero.

The misleading "framework is not installed" error is translated once, in machinery, under test. No operator will ever run `daana-cli install` against a busy file and start deleting schemas to make it work.

Keeping UPPER_SNAKE_CASE keeps the one file where business and source vocabulary meet — the mapping — legible at a glance, which is the only remaining enforcement of "no source name appears anywhere in DAB" now that daana-cli 0.7.0 has deleted its casing lint rules.

FULL_LOG re-reads the entire retained history of das__staged on every execute. At 830 Northwind orders this is free; at the first source with a daily full extract, execute time grows linearly with days retained and never comes back down. The escape — TRANSACTIONAL or INCREMENTAL — costs us the reproducibility property above and buys the batch_history abort path documented in `execute --help` (prior 'F'/'R' rows with no 'C' abort the pipeline and need manual repair), so the fix for the slow build is strictly worse than the build.

We have engineered FULL_LOG's soft-delete into never firing. It deletes when a key disappears from the source view; our staged view is append-only over the whole lake, so a key never disappears. An order deleted at the source stays in `dab.view_ORDER` forever and nothing in the build will say so. We have chosen a mechanism whose delete semantics are structurally unreachable, and no test can detect the miss, because the correct answer is indistinguishable from the wrong one without going back to the source — which S2 forbids.

The build is now strictly serial and hostile to a human being present. A marimo page left open, an editor's database viewer, or a second developer's `duckdb` REPL turns a ten-second build into a failure, and the failure is only intelligible because of a string match against a nightly binary's error text that we now own and must keep in step. The day the vendor rewords that message, our test goes red and someone has to go and find out what the new wording is.

The engine is an unversioned nightly pinned by content hash on a branch we do not control. If that branch is force-pushed or the LFS object is garbage-collected, the pinned bytes become unfetchable and there is no upstream to ask for them — we have no version number with which to request the same build again. The mitigation (a cached copy, `DAANA_CLI` pointing at it) is a copy someone has to have kept.

The pin is `linux-amd64`. The DAB layer is verified on exactly one platform; a developer on macOS arm64 cannot build DAB at all until a second object is pinned, and the build must fail loudly rather than silently skipping the layer. This is a real barrier to a second person joining the work.

Keeping UPPER_SNAKE_CASE keeps two casing worlds, which is why `RF06` — table-qualification of column references, the one sqlfluff correctness rule that cannot be autofixed — stays excluded for *all* SQL in the repository, hand-written included. We pay that price on every file to buy legibility in the mapping files.

Banning `view_<ENTITY>_with_rel` means DAR gets relationship keys one relationship view at a time: n reads for n edges rather than one wide read per entity. Slice 1 has no relationships so the cost is zero now and grows with every edge added, and the ban is a rule rather than a mechanism — nothing in DuckDB stops someone reading `_focal` and getting a confident, empty, plausible answer.

`PLACED_ON` is declared `START_TIMESTAMP` because the DMDL vocabulary has no plain timestamp. If the engine treats START/END_TIMESTAMP as a validity interval rather than an instant, a `START_TIMESTAMP` with no matching `END_TIMESTAMP` may be rejected or may acquire behaviour we did not ask for. We are relying on a semantic reading of five type names, and the first slice is where we find out.

data.contextAndProblem:
DAB is the layer the whole architecture exists for. It is where meaning is defined exactly once (blueprint B8), where change must be additive (B7), and where history must be retained such that an answer served last quarter is reproducible this quarter (B3). We have decided that daana-cli produces it, that `dab/model.yaml` is the only place the data is explained, and that the physical target is one DuckDB file. That decision is not in question here. What is in question is everything that makes it survivable: where the binary comes from, what a mapping file is allowed to say, who is allowed to have the file open, and what DAR is allowed to see of what the engine produced.

The first hard thing is that this engine has no version. Its own `-v` prints `daana-cli version nightly, commit 113d5a6a77c123679656a9c769c6b88123341f36, built at 2026-09-04T22:13:46Z`. There is no semver to depend on, no release to request again, and the artefact lives as a 174 MB git-LFS object on a branch called `binaries` in a repository we do not control. Its `--help` advertises "Multi-database support (PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, Oracle, SQL Server)" and does not list DuckDB. The 0.7.0 release post names PostgreSQL and BigQuery as the only tested environments. So the platform we have chosen is unadvertised, unsupported territory in an unversioned nightly build — and it works, fully, as spike 2 proved end to end. Everything below follows from taking that pair of facts seriously at the same time.

The second hard thing is that the engine accepts wrong mappings without complaining, and one class of wrongness corrupts the warehouse invisibly and irreversibly. Spike 2 set `ingestion_strategy: FULL` against a staged view holding two rows for one key and watched `CUSTOMER_desc` grow 22 → 23 → 24 → 25, one duplicate row per execute, forever — while `view_CUSTOMER` stayed at 3 rows and `view_CUSTOMER_hist` at 4 throughout. The corruption never reaches a consumer, so nothing downstream can detect it, and switching the strategy back stops the growth but does not clean up what leaked. This is not an exotic edge case in our design: spike 1 established that dlt's append disposition over a partitioned lake means `das__staged` holds more than one row per key *by construction* ("Two identical runs produce 240 rows for 120 distinct orders"). The default-looking strategy is the one that destroys the layer. That single fact determines the shape of this record: the honesty of DAB is exactly equal to the rules we impose on the mapping files, plus the tests that check them, because the engine will not.

The third hard thing is concurrency, and it is worse than it sounds. Spike 2 found that if any other process holds the `.duckdb` file open — "read-write OR READ-ONLY" — `daana-cli execute` fails with "daana framework is not installed on the remote database. Run 'daana-cli install' first", and the real lock error "is swallowed and does not appear even at `--log-level debug`". In this architecture the things that will hold that file open are the marimo page reading `dar__uss`, a dlt run, and a developer's REPL — i.e. the normal state of the world. An operator who believes the message will run `install` against a live warehouse. The problem is not just to serialise the build; it is that the diagnostic actively points at a destructive wrong answer.

The fourth is that the engine's physical output on DuckDB is partly a trap. `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` are created and never populated — zero rows for both entities — while `execute` still reports its `execute_idfr_pipelines` phase as succeeding. The presentation views are thin wrappers over DuckDB **table macros**, which do not appear in `information_schema.tables` at all. And `view_<entity>_with_rel`, whose name promises the relationship keys joined on, has a column list "byte-identical to `view_<entity>`" and carries none. Every one of those produces a plausible, silent, wrong answer rather than an error. DAR is generated code reading DAB; if it is written against the wrong objects it will emit zeroes with total confidence.

The fifth is a convention under pressure. conventions.md §1.2 makes UPPER_SNAKE_CASE with `id` == `name` a hard rule. daana-cli 0.7.0 removed its enforcement of exactly that — "Entity IDs, workflow IDs, attribute names, and relationship names now accept any casing" — and deleted the three lint rules that checked it. Spike 2 then showed what our platform does with it: DuckDB *preserves* the casing, producing `view_CUSTOMER`, `CUSTOMER_desc`, `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x`, where the same model on PostgreSQL folds to lowercase. So a rule the tool no longer supports now also produces platform-dependent object names in a system whose whole point is that the platform sits behind one seam. Either the convention earns its keep against that, or it should be superseded rather than left as folklore.
decisionDrivers: CI must build the whole spine from recorded fixtures on a runner that has never seen the engine, and every commit must pass the gate on its own (conventions §7) or bisect is worthless
The engine self-reports as `nightly` with no semantic version, so its identity can only be its content
DuckDB is not an advertised or tested target of this engine; every DuckDB-specific behaviour we rely on is unmaintained territory and must be pinned by a test rather than trusted
The engine accepts several kinds of wrong mapping silently, and one of them corrupts a base table invisibly and irreversibly
Blueprint B8: meaning is defined exactly once, in DAB — so anything a mapping expression silently decides is a second, invisible definition
Blueprint S2: DAB must be rebuildable from DAS at any time, which constrains what das__staged may look like and therefore which ingestion strategy is legal
Only one process may hold the DuckDB file, and the engine's diagnostic for that condition points at a destructive wrong answer
Blueprint R4 and F2: DAR is generated and reads only DAB, so what it may read has to be an explicit allow-list rather than whatever the catalog happens to expose
The whole layer must stay replaceable — nothing above DAB may depend on daana's physical shapes (blueprint preamble: every tool must be replaceable without invalidating a line of the blueprint)

notSettled: Whether FULL_LOG reconstructs the complete version history in a single cold execute from a staged view that already holds every version, or only accumulates versions across successive executes. Spike 2 proved stability under a multi-row source (runs 7-8 byte-stable) and proved multi-execute historization (finding 6), but never rebuilt from an empty warehouse against a source already holding two versions. Every CI run is exactly that scenario, so slice 1 finds out immediately — which is why the confirmation test seeds two extraction dates.

What the engine actually does with `type: "START_TIMESTAMP"` on an attribute with no matching END_TIMESTAMP. The DMDL vocabulary has no plain timestamp type, so PLACED_ON has no unambiguously correct declaration. Spike 2's ORDER entity did materialise `order_purchase_ts TIMESTAMP`, but the model.yaml that produced it was copied from the quickstart and never shown, so the DMDL type behind that column is unknown. If START_TIMESTAMP turns out to declare a validity interval rather than an instant, the fallback is STRING carrying ISO-8601 with the cast in DAR — a worse answer that would need registering.

Whether the relationship view name is `view_<SOURCE>_<NAME>_<TARGET>` composed by the engine (making the id the bare verb phrase `IS_PLACED_BY`) or `view_<relationship_id>` (making the id the whole sentence). Spike 2 observed `view_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER` without showing the model, and the 0.7.0 post writes the template as `view_<source>_has_<target>` with `has` literal, which is consistent with either reading. M9 assumes composition; the emitted name is asserted by a test on first deploy rather than assumed, and if the assumption is wrong the fix is one line in model.yaml.

Whether two relationships between the same ordered entity pair collide in the `<SOURCE>_<TARGET>_x` cross table, which carries no relationship name. Neither the spike nor the blog exercises it. M11 forbids the second edge pending evidence; the day a slice needs ORDER→CUSTOMER twice (placed-by and shipped-to), someone has to test it.

What FULL_LOG does when a key disappears from the staged view. Spike 2 ran out of time-box: "does FULL tombstone/close the row (row_st flips from 'Y'), or does the entity stay in view_<entity> forever? The _desc table has row_st, sta_tmstp and end_tmstp columns that are all currently 'Y'/NULL/NULL, so the machinery for it exists — but I did not exercise it." In our design the case never arises, which is precisely the problem recorded in the consequences.

Whether `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` are populated on PostgreSQL. Only DuckDB was observed, both empty. If PostgreSQL populates them this is a DuckDB defect worth reporting and worth guarding against in the DAR generator; if not, they are vestigial. Either way M14's allow-list holds, but the reason for it changes.

Whether `type_key` is stable across a drop-and-redeploy. 0.7.0 says the values are read from metadata tables at Function DDL time "rather than sequential counters" but states no stability guarantee. M14 keeps DAR off `_desc`/`_x` so it does not matter today; it will matter the first time anyone wants incremental DAR builds keyed on those tables.

Whether the relative `database:` path is resolved against the process cwd or against the connections.yaml location. M12 makes the two coincide so the question cannot bite, but that is avoidance rather than an answer, and it constrains where connections.yaml may live.

The exact key names of workflow.yaml and config.yaml. Neither was captured verbatim by the spike. The rule (produce them with `daana-cli generate`, then edit) converts the gap into a procedure, but the first person to write them will discover the real schema.

Whether "CI is offline" is scoped to the source system or means no network at all. This decision reads it as the former — CI already reaches PyPI on every `uv sync --frozen` — and fetching the engine from GitHub is the same class of network call. If it hardens to the latter, the manifest already supports a pre-seeded cache or DAANA_CLI, but the acquisition option changes and this record should be superseded rather than reinterpreted.

Where relationship cardinality lives. The USS generator needs typed n:1 / 1:n / m:n edges and DMDL has no cardinality key, so it must go in the dab/uss.yaml sidecar — which means a DAB fact lives outside model.yaml, straining B8's "meaning is defined exactly once, here". Slice 1 has no relationships, so the strain is deferred, not resolved.

Whether two concurrent daana-cli invocations conflict. Spike 2 did not test it but noted that "given that even a read-only holder breaks it, they will almost certainly conflict". The single-writer lock makes it moot for our build; it would matter the day someone wants to parallelise entities across processes.

Whether the daana-cli licence permits redistribution. It bears directly on the rejected vendoring option and was not established; if redistribution is permitted and LFS bandwidth is later solved, vendoring becomes cheaper than it looks here.
